title: The Power Grab of the AI Doomers
content:
This new UnHerd magazine essay is about the authoritarian politics of AI Doomerism. It explains how it turned philosophical thought experiments into proposals for mass surveillance of researchers.
EARLIER this week, cybersecurity experts discovered something nasty online: two critical flaws in PHP, the code that has been used to build approximately two-thirds of the World Wide Web. On Tuesday, various European governments shut down websites as they scrambled to fix the flaws before malign actors were able to exploit them. Millions more websites will now need to be “patched”. “For the big juicy targets, I hope to goodness they are being patched quickly,” said one cybersecurity expert.
In this case, AI might just have saved the day. The flaws were discovered because cybersecurity experts used AI to search for weaknesses that humans had missed. Had, say, AI-assisted Russian cybercriminals gotten there first, it might have been far worse. The incident gives an insight into the double-edged nature of AI, which presents clear and present dangers, but also new tools to combat those dangers. Note, however, that we are talking about the fairly unsexy business of cybercrime and not, for example, sentient computers spontaneously deciding to eradicate humanity or farming our living souls in some sort of Matrix nightmare. And yet it is these scenarios, dreamed up by a small set of extravagantly funded AI Doomers and spread by a credulous media, that have been occupying the world’s attention — going into overdrive since the OpenAI “Hugging Face” hack and Jacob Coxon’s resignation from Anthropic went viral.
For “normies,” anxiety about a new emerging technology tends to center on things like jobs, education, or the economy. Cybersecurity experts tend to worry about tangible threats to existing systems. But AI Doomerism is distinct. It describes people who believe that advanced AI poses a risk of human extinction. They are, generally, prepared to put a number on it. Coxon’s former colleague Evan Hubinger set his own “p(doom)” at “above 10%”; some go as high as 25% or even 50%.
Much has been written about the strange confluence of money, power, and quasi-theological belief systems that have given rise to this apocalyptic worldview. Still, what receives less attention is what this movement actually wants to happen in order to avert this scenario, which is to say, the authoritarian and even totalitarian implications of the AI Doomers’ policy proposals. Ideas of mass surveillance that would make Big Brother blush have almost imperceptibly crept from the fantastical thought experiments of Effective Altruists and the Rationalists and are now being turned into policy proposals by such figures as Bernie Sanders.
To understand the peculiar flavor of AI Doomerism, a good place to start is a 2019 TED talk given by Oxford’s Nick Bostrom, one of the leading philosophers on existential risks, titled “How civilization could destroy itself—and 4 ways we could prevent it.” Bostrom opened his talk with a thought experiment. He asked his audience to imagine an urn containing various balls representing technological advances. There would be some white balls, representing beneficial discoveries. There would be some grey balls, representing discoveries that have some positive and some negative benefits. But there might be a few black balls: discoveries so profound, they would effectively make political life as we know it unsustainable. One example might be synthetic biology: imagine if your average supervillain really did gain the ability to create mutants! Another might be general artificial intelligence.
Bostrom’s point was that once the ball is withdrawn from the urn, you can’t put it back. Therefore, the only viable technological safeguard would be to stop anyone from withdrawing any black balls in the first place. And the only real way of doing this, he mused, was: “Ubiquitous surveillance — everybody would be monitored all the time.” The interviewer’s thoughts turned immediately to Hollywood: “This is Minority Report, essentially.” Bostrom duly admitted that there were “huge problems and risks” associated with the idea of mass surveillance and global governance. But perhaps, he mused, people would be more willing to wear multidirectional cameras and microphones if we called this “The ‘freedom tag’… or something like that.” Still, he suggested that “we seemed to be doomed anyway,” by which logic, extreme solutions may come to seem proportionate.
Over time, this “end justifies the means” mindset moved from thought experiment to policy proposal, with increasingly concrete ideas for controlling AI research and the people working on it. With the work of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI), the case for totalizing enforcement became more explicit.
MIRI is a Berkeley-based nonprofit organization, founded more than two decades ago by the writer Eliezer Yudkowsky and backed by a remarkable concentration of money and influence. Its funders include Open Philanthropy, the philanthropic organization founded by Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz and Cari Tuna; Vitalik Buterin, the co-founder of Ethereum (an open-source blockchain); and Jaan Tallinn, the Estonian programmer who helped build Skype and has since made existential risk one of the central objects of his philanthropy. Tallinn is a particularly important figure in this ecosystem: through the Survival and Flourishing Fund, which he funds alongside other philanthropists, he has helped direct hundreds of millions of dollars towards organizations concerned with AI existential risks.
MIRI’s particular obsession is artificial superintelligence (ASI) — a hypothetical scenario in which computers develop vastly superior intelligence to humans on every vector. Its position on ASI is: “Everyone dies.” Yudkowsky therefore argues that the only reasonable response is a globally coordinated and collectively enforced moratorium on the development of ASI.
This may not worry you, since you (I assume) have no intention of trying to create ASI. But the wider problem is enforcement. If governments agree to halt this kind of research, how do they know companies or individuals are obeying? In June, MIRI’s Technical Governance Team published Verifying Restrictions on Frontier AI Research, which considers how such a prohibition could actually be policed. The paper catalogs 28 possible verification mechanisms, including intelligence gathering; international search warrants and inspections (of properties, computers, and files); polygraphs; monitoring what users type into AI systems and what the model produces while it is being used; sting operations; employee-monitoring software; and AI-assisted code review, which may extend to codebases, experiment logs, and research documents. It is a proposal for giving governments unprecedented oversight of private activity. Researchers would work under permanent clouds of suspicion, never knowing which of their experiments might be deemed illicit, which conversations were incriminating, which of their colleagues was an informant.
This really is a dystopian nightmare, and, unfortunately, not the dystopia the media is covering.
Journalists have spent years asking readers to imagine the dictatorship of future machines while paying far less attention to the systems of human control being proposed to prevent it.
MIRI itself acknowledged that such mechanisms could “enable authoritarianism” and cautioned that some “might be undesirable.” And yet, thanks to the well-funded ecosystem of organizations surrounding MIRI, these ideas have now migrated into public policy proposals.

report.summary: A new UnHerd essay argues AI doomers' extinction fears have quietly mutated into proposals for mass surveillance of AI researchers — and now into real legislation.
report.background: AI doomerism grew out of the Effective Altruism and Rationalist communities, where thinkers like Oxford's Nick Bostrom and MIRI founder Eliezer Yudkowsky framed superintelligence as a potential extinction-level 'black ball' that cannot be un-invented. That framing attracted serious money: Open Philanthropy (funded by Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz), Ethereum's Vitalik Buterin and Skype's Jaan Tallinn have collectively steered hundreds of millions of dollars toward existential-risk work. For years these were thought experiments. But as p(doom) estimates — 10%, 25%, even 50% — went mainstream and the media amplified OpenAI and Anthropic drama, the movement's policy arm matured. Simultaneously, AI is proving genuinely useful against mundane threats: cybersecurity researchers recently used it to find critical PHP vulnerabilities before criminals did, a reminder that concrete risks and speculative ones are not the same thing.
key_points: Real versus imagined threats: AI recently helped security experts uncover two critical PHP flaws underpinning much of the web, a tangible win. Yet public attention is fixated on sentient-machine apocalypse scenarios promoted by a small, extravagantly funded group — not on cybercrime, jobs, or the boring, genuine dangers.

Bostrom's 'urn' thought experiment: if a civilisation-ending discovery is drawn, it cannot be put back — so the only safeguard is preventing anyone from drawing it. His proposed answer, floated in a 2019 TED talk, was ubiquitous surveillance, perhaps rebranded as a 'freedom tag' to make it palatable.

From philosophy to policy machinery: MIRI's Technical Governance Team published a paper cataloguing 28 verification mechanisms for an ASI moratorium — intelligence gathering, international inspections, polygraphs, sting operations, employee-monitoring software, and AI-assisted review of code, logs and documents.

A well-funded pipeline: MIRI, founded by Eliezer Yudkowsky and backed by Tallinn, Moskovitz and Buterin, sits inside an ecosystem that has moved ideas from blog posts into draft legislation, with MIRI itself conceding its mechanisms could 'enable authoritarianism'.

Legislative momentum: Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Greg Casar introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, which would permanently prohibit ASI development and pause frontier AI work until a new federal regulator enforces the ban.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this reframes the safety debate: the near-term policy risk may not be overregulation of models but a surveillance apparatus aimed at the researchers themselves — inspections, polygraphs, informants and keystroke monitoring. Labs and startups would operate under permanent suspicion, with compliance costs and legal ambiguity chilling open research. For developers, the practical worry is that verification regimes extend to codebases, experiment logs and internal communications, turning ordinary engineering into potential evidence. For ordinary users, the more relevant threats remain fraud, insecure infrastructure and job disruption — problems AI can help solve as well as cause. The deeper impact is narrative: years of attention spent imagining machine dictators has crowded out scrutiny of the human control systems being built in their name.
report.tools: Read the original UnHerd essay and MIRI's 'Verifying Restrictions on Frontier AI Research' for the primary proposals. Follow governance and evaluation work at METR, Apollo Research and the UK AI Safety Institute's Inspect framework, plus policy trackers covering the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act. Open Philanthropy and the Survival and Flourishing Fund's grant lists reveal who funds this ecosystem. For the concrete-risk side, watch AI-assisted vulnerability discovery tools from firms like XBOW and Google's Big Sleep.
